snip.t: Renal & endocrine history: “Do you have known kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, thyroid or adrenal problems?” — CKD, diabetic nephropathy, primary hyperaldosteronism, Addison’s disease, hyperparathyroidism are common causes.
| Hyperparathyroidism | Hypercalcaemia, bone pain | Elevated PTH, renal stones; no monoclonal spike, bone changes are subperiosteal. |
Side effects: tremor, thirst and polyuria (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), weight gain, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism), GI upset, chronic kidney disease.

Hypercalcaemia: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy (bone metastases, PTH‑rP), granulomatous disease (TB), excessive vitamin D — Disseminated TB (granulomatous production of 1‑α‑hydroxylase), HIV‑associated lymphoma, sickle‑cell osteonecrosis
Bone pain, pruritus, restless legs: Secondary hyperparathyroidism, calcium‑phosphate imbalance and uremic neuropathy.
Bone tenderness, calcific deposits in soft tissues: Secondary hyperparathyroidism leading to renal osteodystrophy and metastatic calcification.
Serum electrolytes, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, PTH: Metabolic complications of CKD — Hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, secondary hyperparathyroidism

o: High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH
High calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
Low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
qs.e: Primary hyperparathyroidism features excess PTH causing hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia due to renal phosphate wasting.

qs.q: The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is
qs.e: Solitary adenoma accounts for ~85% of primary HPT. Four-gland hyperplasia = ~15%. Parathyroid carcinoma = <1%. Primary HPT is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in outpatients (vs malignancy = most common in inpatients).

qs.q: Secondary hyperparathyroidism is most often due to
qs.e: CRF mechanism: decreased GFR → phosphate retention (hyperphosphatemia) + decreased 1-alpha hydroxylation of vitamin D → hypocalcemia → all four parathyroid glands undergo compensatory hyperplasia → elevated PTH. This is a REACTIVE (compensatory) process, not autonomous.

o: A parathyroid adenoma metastasizing to distant sites
Chronically hyperplastic parathyroids developing autonomous function
Thyroid surgery accidentally removing all parathyroids
Autoantibodies destroying parathyroid tissue over time
qs.e: After prolonged secondary HPT, one or more hyperplastic glands undergoes monoclonal transformation → autonomous PTH secretion independent of calcium feedback → hypercalcemia develops even after the original cause (e.g. CRF) is corrected (e.g. post-renal transplant). May require parathyroidectomy.

qs.q: The classic symptomatic triad of primary hyperparathyroidism is
o: Bones, stones, groans, and psychic moans
qs.e: Bones (osteitis fibrosa cystica, subperiosteal resorption, brown tumors), Stones (nephrolithiasis — calcium oxalate/phosphate), Groans (peptic ulcers, constipation, nausea — hypercalcemia reduces smooth muscle tone), Psychic moans (depression, confusion, lethargy). Today most cases are asymptomatic, found incidentally.

qs.q: Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor (HPT-JT) syndrome involves germline mutations in
o: Mutations in the cyclin D1 gene
qs.e: HPT-JT syndrome: CDC73 germline mutations → parathyroid tumors (often cystic adenomas, higher risk of carcinoma ~15%) + ossifying fibromas of jaw + renal lesions (cysts, hamartomas, Wilms tumor). Important to recognize because of elevated carcinoma risk vs sporadic HPT.

qs.q: First-line management of asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism without meeting surgical criteria is
o: Observation with monitoring of key parameters
Vitamin D supplementation as sole therapy
qs.e: Surgical criteria (any one): calcium >0.25mmol/L above upper normal, age <50, eGFR <60, T-score <−2.5 or fragility fracture, 24hr urine calcium >400mg. If none met → watchful waiting: annual calcium/creatinine, 1–3 yearly DEXA scan. Avoid thiazides, lithium, immobilization, high calcium diet.

qs.q: A patient with severe hyperparathyroidism undergoing parathyroidectomy suddenly develops tetany and carpopedal spasm post-operatively. This is most consistent with
o: Hypocalcemia due to hungry bone syndrome
qs.e: Hungry bone syndrome occurs post-parathyroidectomy in patients with severe HPT and high bone turnover. The abrupt removal of PTH leads to rapid bone mineralization, causing a precipitous drop in serum calcium. Tetany and carpopedal spasm are classic signs of hypocalcemia.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hyperparathyroidism is excess parathyroid hormone causing high calcium and low phosphate. It can be primary (autonomous gland) or secondary (reactive to low calcium). Diagnosis relies on calcium, phosphate, PTH levels and imaging.

sections.p: Hyperparathyroidism is defined by elevated serum PTH with discordant calcium: primary shows hypercalcemia, secondary shows normal/low calcium. Diagnosis requires at least two abnormal labs and exclusion of other causes.

t.b: Is calcium high, normal, or low? High suggests primary; low/normal suggests secondary or tertiary.
Is phosphate low, normal, or high? Low in primary; high in secondary.
Is PTH elevated? Confirms hyperparathyroidism; suppressed PTH points to non‑parathyroid hypercalcemia.
Is vitamin D deficient? Deficiency supports secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Localizes adenoma or hyperplasia when surgery is considered; if unavailable, rely on clinical and lab picture.

sections.p: Severity is staged by serum calcium level and end‑organ effects. Mild: calcium <12 mg/dL, no symptoms. Moderate: 12‑14 mg/dL or bone pain. Severe: >14 mg/dL, nephrolithiasis, pancreatitis, neuro‑cognitive changes.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is most often a solitary parathyroid adenoma. Secondary causes include chronic kidney disease, vitamin D deficiency, and malabsorption. In low‑resource settings, consider HIV‑associated nephropathy and TB‑related renal disease.
Patients may have bone pain, fractures, kidney stones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric “stones”. Many are asymptomatic and discovered on routine labs.
Lab and imaging confirm diagnosis and assess complications.
b: Calcium, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D, creatinine

t.b: Is urinary calcium high? Helps differentiate primary from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia; high supports primary.
Is bone density reduced? Indicates skeletal involvement and guides surgery timing.
Are stones or nephrocalcinosis present? Detects renal complications.

sections.p: Life‑threatening complications include severe hypercalcemia (>14 mg/dL), cardiac arrhythmias, pancreatitis, and renal failure.
Treat the underlying cause, control calcium, and consider surgery for primary disease. Use hydration, bisphosphonates, or calcimimetics when needed.
b: IV saline hydration to promote calciuresis

sections.p: Monitor calcium, phosphate, PTH, renal function, and bone density every 6–12 months. Prevent fractures with calcium/vitamin D supplementation and weight‑bearing exercise.
Conditions that cause hypercalcemia or elevated PTH can mimic hyperparathyroidism.
Vitamin D deficiency can mask primary disease by lowering calcium; renal failure can elevate PTH without true hyperparathyroidism.
b: Low vitamin D → normal calcium despite adenoma

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypercalcemia with confusion, arrhythmia, or pancreatitis
Sudden onset of kidney stone pain
Rapidly worsening bone pain or fractures

faq.q: How to differentiate primary from secondary hyperparathyroidism?
faq.a: Primary: high PTH with hypercalcemia and low phosphate. Secondary: high PTH with low/normal calcium and high phosphate, often due to CKD or vitamin D deficiency.
High urinary calcium supports primary disease; low urinary calcium suggests familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, a benign mimic.
When calcium >1 mg/dL above normal, symptomatic bone/renal disease, age <50, or a >1 cm adenoma on imaging.
